title: Remove Zero Sum Consecutive Nodes from Linked List
description: Brute force to optimized: repeatedly rescanning and removing versus a two-pass prefix-sum hash map that handles cascading removals directly.

sections.title: Remove Zero Sum Consecutive Nodes from Linked List

content.title: Remove Zero Sum Consecutive Nodes from Linked List

blocks.text: Given the head of a linked list, repeatedly delete consecutive sequences of nodes that sum to 0 until there are no such sequences remaining. Return the head of the final list. (More than one valid answer may exist; any correct one is accepted.)

blocks.caption: Whenever the running prefix sum repeats, the span between those two repeats sums to exactly 0 and can be removed

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","The head of a singly linked list of integers"],["Output","The head of the list after removing every zero-summing consecutive span"],["Goal","Remove all zero-sum spans efficiently in effectively one pass, rather than repeatedly rescanning"],["Constraints","The number of nodes is in the range [1, 1000]; -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Consecutive sequence sums to 0\"","The classic prefix-sum trick: a span sums to zero exactly when its prefix sum repeats a value seen before"],["Sequences can be removed and then MORE zero-sum sequences can appear from the remaining pieces","Using the LAST occurrence of each prefix sum (not the first) automatically handles this cascading removal in a single pass"]]}

blocks.text: Any consecutive span of nodes whose values sum to exactly 0 should be deleted; this may need to happen repeatedly, since removing one span could bring together nodes that ALSO now sum to zero as a combined span.

blocks.title: Analogy: Canceling Out Debts and Credits in a Transaction Log
blocks.text: Imagine a running log of transactions (deposits and withdrawals) in order. Any CONSECUTIVE block of transactions that nets out to exactly zero can be erased entirely from the log, as if it never happened. Cleverly, this can be spotted by tracking the RUNNING TOTAL after each transaction: if the running total ever returns to a value it had before, everything in between summed to zero and can be erased in one shot, without needing to repeatedly rescan.

blocks.caption: A hash map from prefix sum to the last node reached with that sum lets any zero-sum span be skipped directly in a single pass

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Prefix sums: 1, 3, 6, 3, 7","The prefix sum 3 repeats (after node valued 2, and again after node valued -3)","Everything strictly between those two points (values 3 and -3) sums to exactly 0"],["Remove that span (values 3, -3)","[1,2,4]","The zero-sum span is deleted entirely"],["Answer","[1,2,4]","Matches the expected result"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Prefix sums: 1, 3, 6, 3, 1","Prefix sum 1 repeats (start, and after node valued -2); prefix sum 3 also repeats","Using the LAST occurrence of prefix sum 1 removes the entire span from the 2nd node all the way to the last node in one shot"],["Answer","[1]","Everything after the very first node collectively sums to zero and is removed"]]}

blocks.text: Before repeatedly rescanning the list for zero-sum spans after every removal (a slow, iterative fixup process), notice that tracking prefix sums and always keeping the LAST node seen at each sum value directly identifies the maximal span to remove in one pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A consecutive span from node A (exclusive) to node B (inclusive) sums to zero exactly when the prefix sum just AFTER A equals the prefix sum just AFTER B (their difference, the span's sum, is then zero).

Observation 2: Building a map from prefix-sum-value to "the node where that prefix sum was reached" lets any later repeat of the same value instantly reveal a zero-sum span.

Observation 3: Crucially, always OVERWRITING the map with the LATEST node at each prefix sum (rather than keeping only the first) ensures that if a span is removed and this creates an EVEN LARGER zero-sum span, the map already reflects the correct final endpoints.

Observation 4: A single first pass builds the complete prefix-sum map; a single second pass then uses it to re-link each node directly past whatever span (if any) sums to zero starting right after it.

Recognizing that using the LAST (not first) occurrence of each prefix sum handles ALL cascading removals simultaneously is the key insight that avoids needing to repeat the process multiple times.
This is the prefix-sum-map technique (the same core idea as Subarray Sum Equals K), adapted to a linked list and applied to REMOVE spans rather than count them.
Repeatedly scan the entire list for ANY consecutive span summing to zero; remove the first one found; repeat this whole process from scratch until no such span exists anywhere.

items: Scan every possible starting index i and ending index j (i <= j), tracking the running sum from i to j.
The moment any span sums to exactly 0, remove it entirely and restart the whole scanning process from the beginning, since the remaining values may now form new zero-sum spans.
Repeat until a full scan finds no more zero-sum spans.

codes.python:
def remove_zero_sum_sublists(values):
    values = values[:]
    changed = True
    while changed:                                                          # keep repeating until no zero-sum span remains
        changed = False
        n = len(values)
        for i in range(n):
            total = 0
            for j in range(i, n):
                total += values[j]
                if total == 0:                                             # found a zero-sum span from i to j
                    values = values[:i] + values[j + 1:]                    # remove that entire span
                    changed = True
                    break
            if changed:
                break
    return values


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(remove_zero_sum_sublists([1, 2, 3, -3, 4]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Restarting the scan from the beginning after every removal is necessary in this brute force, since a removal can create brand new adjacencies (and thus new zero-sum spans) anywhere in the list.
The nested loop directly checks every possible (i, j) span using a running total, the most straightforward way to detect a zero-sum span.

blocks.text: Eventually removes every zero-sum span, including cascading ones created by earlier removals, since it fully restarts after each single removal.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^3) in the worst case: O(n^2) to find one span, potentially repeated O(n) times as removals cascade.
Space: O(n), for the working array.

Limitation: repeatedly rescanning from scratch after every single removal is highly wasteful; the prefix-sum-map technique identifies and removes ALL zero-sum spans (including cascading ones) using only two linear passes total.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force restarts its entire scan after every single removal. Instead, recognize that a repeated prefix sum ALWAYS marks a zero-sum span, and using the LAST node seen at each prefix sum value (overwriting earlier ones as the list is walked) automatically produces the correct FINAL span boundaries, even accounting for cascading removals, without ever needing to actually restart.

Use a dummy head (representing prefix sum 0, "before the list starts"). First pass: walk the list once, accumulating a running sum and recording (overwriting) the LAST node reached at each sum value in a hash map. Second pass: walk the list again with a fresh running sum; at each node, re-link its next pointer to seen[currentSum].next, directly skipping over any zero-sum span that starts right after it.
Track prefix sums in a hash map (keeping the last node at each sum), then re-link every node to skip past whatever zero-sum span (if any) follows it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node","Prefix sum","Map after this node"],"rows":[["(dummy)","0","{0: dummy}"],["1","1","{0: dummy, 1: node(1)}"],["2","3","{0: dummy, 1: node(1), 3: node(2)}"],["3","6","{..., 6: node(3)}"],["-3","3","{..., 3: node(-3)}  (overwrites the earlier node(2) entry)"],["-2","1","{..., 1: node(-2)}  (overwrites the earlier node(1) entry)"]]}

blocks.title: Second pass re-linking
blocks.text: At dummy (sum=0): dummy.next = seen[0].next = node(-2).next = null. So the result is just [1] (the dummy links directly to node valued 1, then that node re-links to seen[1].next = null, terminating). Final answer: [1], matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def remove_zero_sum_sublists(head):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    seen = {0: dummy}                                                       # prefix sum 0 corresponds to "before the list starts"

    total = 0
    node = dummy.next
    while node:
        total += node.val
        seen[total] = node                                                  # always keep the LAST node seen with this exact prefix sum
        node = node.next

    total = 0
    node = dummy
    while node:
        total += node.val
        node.next = seen[total].next                                        # jump directly past everything summing to zero in between
        node = node.next
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(-3, ListNode(-2)))))
    result = remove_zero_sum_sublists(head)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two linear passes total.
Space: O(n), for the prefix-sum hash map.

Overwriting the map with the LAST node seen at each prefix sum value is the crucial detail: it guarantees that during the second pass, seen[currentSum] always points to the FURTHEST node sharing the current running sum, meaning node.next = seen[currentSum].next skips over the LARGEST possible zero-sum span starting at that point, correctly handling cascading removals without ever needing to physically restart the process.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A prefix sum value never repeats","seen[sum] simply refers to the current node itself, so its \"next\" link is left unchanged"],["A prefix sum value repeats (possibly several times)","Since the map holds the LAST occurrence, re-linking directly skips the entire (possibly cascaded) zero-sum span in one step"],["The prefix sum returns to 0","This means everything from the true start up to that point sums to zero and gets removed via the dummy node's entry in the map"]]}

items: The dummy node is seeded into the map at prefix sum 0, correctly representing "the state before any node has been included."
The first pass ONLY builds the map (overwriting as needed); no re-linking happens yet, since the map must be COMPLETE before any skipping decisions are made.
The second pass re-computes the running sum independently and uses the now-complete map to perform every re-link in a single linear scan.

blocks.text: Detecting a zero-sum consecutive span (in an array or a linked list) is a direct application of the prefix-sum trick; keeping the LAST occurrence of each prefix sum value (rather than the first) elegantly handles cascading removals without any need to repeat the process.

items: Keeping only the FIRST occurrence of each prefix sum, which fails to correctly handle cascading zero-sum spans created by earlier (conceptual) removals.
Forgetting the dummy node (representing prefix sum 0 before the list starts), which is needed to correctly handle a zero-sum span starting from the true head.
Performing the re-linking DURING the first pass (while the map is still incomplete), rather than in a separate second pass.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["No zero-sum span exists anywhere","Every prefix sum is unique; the second pass leaves every next pointer unchanged"],["The entire list sums to zero","The dummy node's prefix sum (0) repeats at the very end, causing the entire list to be removed"],["Multiple overlapping/cascading zero-sum spans","Correctly collapsed into their maximal combined span by the \"keep the last occurrence\" rule"]]}

items: Explicitly connecting this problem to the more commonly seen "Subarray Sum Equals K" prefix-sum pattern demonstrates strong pattern transfer, even though this problem REMOVES spans rather than counting them.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Consecutive sequence sums to zero" (especially with possible CASCADING removals) points toward a prefix-sum hash map, specifically keeping the LAST occurrence of each sum value.

items: How does this connect to the standard "Subarray Sum Equals K" problem? Both rely on the exact same prefix-sum-repeats-means-zero-sum-span insight, just applied to removal here instead of counting.

Why must the LAST (not first) occurrence of each prefix sum be kept? Keeping the first occurrence would miss larger, cascaded zero-sum spans that only become apparent by considering the furthest matching point.

How would you adapt this if the list were doubly linked? The same two-pass technique applies directly, with the added step of correctly reconnecting each remaining node's "previous" pointer during the second pass.
A direct linked-list adaptation of the prefix-sum technique also seen in Subarray Sum Equals K and related array problems, repurposed here for span REMOVAL rather than counting.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^3) time (worst case), O(n) space.
Optimized (prefix-sum map, two passes): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Prefix-sum hash map (keeping the last occurrence of each sum)
Core Idea: A repeated prefix sum marks a zero-sum span; always keeping the LAST node at each sum value correctly resolves cascading removals in just two linear passes
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Overwriting (not preserving) earlier entries in the prefix-sum map is what correctly handles cascading zero-sum spans without repeated rescans
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Build a prefix-sum map (last node wins), then re-link node.next = map[currentSum].next in a second pass
